title: The fool, the bad and the holy: keen similarities between Fargo (1996) and No Country for Old Men (2007)

commenti.body: Those are some good observations/ Another interesting similarity came all the way back in “Raising Arizona” (not their first film, but the one that put everyone on notice). [The bounty hunter biker character](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=CQ67ZyZtKjU&pp=ygUXUmFpc2luZyBhcmlzb25hIGRyZWFtcyA%3D) is extremely Chigurh-esque in the way he’s both a real character as well as a quasi-analogue for Death itself.

Your understanding of No Country is incorrect. Llewelyn isn’t a fool and there is nothing to suggest he is stupid.

His downfall is he has a code of ethics, he’s an honest man and he goes back to the crime scene.

The way Josh Brolin speaks about his character Llewelyn steals the money to provide a better life for his wife. He is unaware of the havoc which is about to destroy their lives. Anton Chigurh destroys anyone and their family if they get in his way, they can be educated or not, they could be innocent or guilty. He is a psychopath.

While you might be able to shoe-horn some similarities together for the two movies the Coen’s adapted No Country from Cormac McCarthy’s novel they didn’t write it unlike their original screenplay for Fargo. They’re both crime films with some similar tropes.

I agree. While the biker character isn’t necessarily presented as a personification of evil, he's also an one-note antagonist that symbolizes human greed and won't stop at nothing to get what he wants. He's also going against characters that are inherently fools: the couple in Arizona kidnaps a baby for selfish reasons and without a clear understanding of the events they will set in motion (like Jerry, like Llewelyn). It’s like the Coens are drawing a line between pitiful criminals and malicious criminals.

He gets the suitcase even though the money doesn’t belong to him because he sees it as a chance to give himself and his wife a better chance. He’s not honest when he takes the money that doesn’t belong to him, but he’s not as deprived of humanity as Chigurh to feel completely remorseless about his acts – just as when Jerry realizes the effect the kidnapping of his wife could have on his son. 

Most of all, though, Ed Tom Bell doesn’t just want to catch Chigurh, but also to prevent Llewelyn from becoming the next victim of this psychopath, even though he has a clear view of Llewelyn’s unlawful actions. Jerry wanted to provided a better life for his family too, without being emasculated by his father-in-law. He thought he could get away with it, just as Llewelyn thought he could beat this malevolent antagonist.

I'm aware the movie was based on a novel, but the final script framed the story in a particular way that's very specific to the Coen's filmography.

yeah Fargo is all about wincing while you watch someone spiral out of control making a situation much worse than it is.  Llewelyn is portrayed as someone involved in a situation spiraling out of control but who is trying to have a moral code.

The villain comparison, also.  they occupy completely different spaces.  They weren't presenting Grimsrud as an absolute evil, just a really mean small town dude.  The intention of both pieces of art are very different

>Llewelyn is portrayed as someone involved in a situation spiraling out of control but who is trying to have a moral code.

My point is that his "moral code" is ultimately foolish, because that's how the danger gets to his front door. That's what separates him from the true, remorseless personification of evil depicted in the movie.

>The villain comparison, also.  they occupy completely different spaces.  They weren't presenting Grimsrud as an absolute evil, just a really mean small town dude.  The intention of both pieces of art are very different

Also... Fargo doesn’t hint at a backstory whatsoever. He’s a guy that’s presented as part of a criminal duo, yet shoots a police officer without blinking an eye while the other criminal tries to bribe the guy. He shoots Jerry’s wife because she was making too much noise. When Marge finds the house at the end of the movie, we’re well aware the fool criminal was killed with an ax by its partner. The entire movie leads us to believe this guy has such a disregard for human life, that we fear for Marge going there alone after him. When she arrests him, she’s devastated to realize everything happened “for a little bit of money”.

Since Fargo was intended as a possible recreation of a real crime, the Coens included Steve Buscemi's character to draw the attention from the stereotypical evil impersonator and make this plot more realistic.

I've seen people try to claim No Country as a western, but to me it's not. Other than its setting, it's more of a 'fiasco' movie similar to Fargo, as you say, or a mixture of the heist, crime, serieal killer movies. In any case, its thematic concerns and moral universe are different than the templates of the western.

For something truly interesting, I suggest watching Sam Peckinpah's The Getaway, with Ali McGraw and Steve McQueen. They are runaways from a heist gone wrong trying to abscond with the loot. What's fascinating is that its plotline and setting are *ver*y similar to No Country. I haven't read the Cormac McCarthy novel, so can't say whether the similarities originate there or in the Coen Bros. screenplay, but it matches up very well, including a hotel shootout at the end -- which, famously, the Coens decide to not show (as we've seen this in the movie before).

I'd say there are clear similarities to their other Texas noir Blood Simple in the questions of justice, morality, and so on, and which established many of the staging and framing of shots that come up again in No Country.

That doesn’t make Moss stupid in the same way as Jerry.

Part of the thrill of No Country is that Moss is actually quite capable. It’s an effective cat-and-mouse chase and even the almighty Chigurh is given a run for his money.

Really, the two films just share some very basic crime story building blocks in the menacing villain, the relatable Joe, and the detective trying to piece it all together.

>the relatable Joe

Jerry is never a relatable Joe. He's pitiful, but not sympathetic as Moss is presented. They are ultimately fools that cause the destruction of their families because they think they can mingle with criminal activities and sucessfuly pull it off.

I somewhat found Fargo to the be the antithesis to No Country, and vice versa. In the former everything that happens is due to the action of the characters. Sure, they all spiral into unintentional consequences, but by the end Marge, who was on top of things the whole time, arrests the perps involved and we get a satisfying ending.

Contrast that with No Country, where characters find money and die out of nowhere due to situations outside of the film's control, and where even Chigurh, the agent of chaos, is not immune to the same rules he inflicts unto others. In Fargo order wins in the end, but in No Country we're left reminiscing a time when it existed, or seemingly existed at least.
If you want to characterize all of those characters as “fools,” then sure, both Moss and Jerry occupy that same very fundamental role in the basic crime flick, as the guy who gets into the jackpot.
I don’t think playing the role of the fool and actually being a stupid fool are all that different.

I guess it also comes down to whether or not you believe that not coming out on top necessarily means you’re a fool.

Is it possible to lose and not be a fool? Because Moss surely took a huge risk for a big reward and came up short. Does that automatically make him a fool?

I read the novel that served as the basis for "NCFOM". And there’s a fundamental change in the adaptation. While Tommy Lee Jones’s character laments that, in the old days, sheriffs didn’t even have to carry guns because the respect for their moral authority was enough, both the novel and the movie acknowledge this as a sign of changing times: not even a gun would be enough for law enforcement to keep a man like Chigurh from causing harm. 

In the novel, however, the overall message is that the values of decency defended by Jones were outdated and doomed to be destroyed. In the movie, while Chigurh also isn’t arrested and held accountable by his crimes, there’s a positive spin in the story, just like it happened in Fargo (where the culprit is indeed apprehended): decency and humanity aren’t all lost, and can be preserved even when facing the horrors that exist out there.

The stories make clear that there was no way they’d come out on top, because they were making impulsive decisions and going against strongest, evil opponents. There’s not much of a difference of how Jerry took a huge risk for a huge reward, and how Llewelyn did the same. They were fools because they underestimated the danger they and their loved ones were putting themselves in when that choice was made.

I think a big difference is that Jerry is actually stupid and incompetent and panicky, whereas Moss is clever and competent and collected.

But as I said in another comment, they both definitely serve as that same basic building block in a crime flick: the guy who gets in the jackpot. I just don’t think there’s anything profound about recognizing that both crime flicks have a cop, a villain, and a guy in the jackpot.

> both the novel and the movie acknowledge this as a sign of changing times: not even a gun would be enough for law enforcement to keep a man like Chigurh from causing harm.

> In the novel, however, the overall message is that the values of decency defended by Jones were outdated and doomed to be destroyed. In the movie, while Chigurh also isn’t arrested and held accountable by his crimes, there’s a positive spin in the story, just like it happened in Fargo (where the culprit is indeed apprehended): decency and humanity aren’t all lost, and can be preserved even when facing the horrors that exist out there.

That’s a massive misreading of both the book and the movie. The whole point is that, while Bell is shocked by the events of the movie and thinks it’s a sign that things are getting worse, the reality is that the world has always been hard on people, full of violence and cruelty. 

The world’s not getting worse, it’s just No Country For Old Men.
The screenplay for the movie follows the novel *very* closely.

>I just don’t think there’s anything profound about recognizing that both crime flicks have a cop, a villain, and a guy in the jackpot.

That wasn't my point.. I sharing a personal reflection about how this triad of characters serve to similar narrative purposes, and you're free to disagree and share your view. Arguments such as "Moss was more skillful than Jerry" don't change my overall view of their archetypes, that's why I kept the conversation going so we could debate.

>the reality is that the world has always been hard on people, full of violence and cruelty.

Tommy Lee Jones and Frances McDormand's character are well aware of this at the end of their movies. The fact is that they're both not defeated by this comprehension, and are able to preserve their humanity. The original novel is much less hopeful in that regard.
You can apply it to Seven too. Somerset is the wise detective and moral center, Doe is the villain, and Mills is the average Joe unknowingly in over his head.

My point is that neither the film nor the movie are claiming that the world is getting worse.

The story is commenting on human nature and saying the *opposite.*

You're the one who brought the Average Joe into question, Brad Pitt in Seven is not a foolish guy mingling in criminal activities and, most of all, there are no evident parallels I can think of with David Fincher's filmography, though I'm genuinely interested to hear your thoughts about that.

Mills is the same level of foolish as Moss. He’s competent and intelligent, but headstrong and leaps into the case thinking there’s no chance he can lose, only to find his adversary more cunning and vicious than he imagined.

My point is that these are very basic crime story building blocks.

>My point is that neither the book nor the movie are claiming that the world is getting worse.

My point wasn't this either. The conclusion of both the movie and the book were the same about the world as it is. The difference is how the book and the movie treat the values of decency. But that's my interpretation, of course!

I directly quoted where you said that both the film and novel were using Bell’s anecdote about an unarmed sheriff as a sign of changing times. And that the story showed that values like decency were outdated.

That’s what *Bell* thinks is happening in the beginning, but that’s not the message of the story.

>Mills is the same level of foolish as Moss. He’s competent and intelligent, but headstrong and leaps into the case thinking there’s no chance he can lose, only to find his adversary more cunning and vicious than he imagined.

One is an inexperienced police officer, the other is a naive criminal. They don't serve the same purpose in their movies. Even if they did, though, you can maybe make a case for how this is a constant theme in David Fincher's thrillers? From what I'm getting, it's almost like you're suggesting that the Coen's make lazy narrative choices for resorting to old tropes

>I directly quoted where you said that both the film and novel were using Bell’s anecdote about an unarmed sheriff as a sign of changing times. And that the story showed that values like decency were outdated.

I stand by it. The character's worldview in the novel is presented as a lost battle. In the movie, there's enough nuance to suggest that, even though we're losing the fight, it's admirable that there are still people out there that keep such values alive.
In my view, they're people that venture into criminal activities to serve their own interests, not because they originally intended to destroy a third party.

It has been a while since I watched the film, but I took the ending as a bit more melancholic. The culprit isn't apprehended, but instead accomplishes his goal of getting rid of everyone involved. Even the closest he's gotten killed wasn't through law enforcement, but instead by the same forces of chaos he symbolizes. It seems important that the ending is Tommy Lee Jones talking about his dreams, cause maybe thats all it ever was: a dream.

It's funny you making a comparison between these two films because I just did a rewatch of NCFOM last week and the "regional argot in rural policing" symmetry really stuck out to me this time. And I've seen NCFOM and Fargo probably a dozen times each and I've never noticed it's "funny talking police" in each as a gimmick.

My take is that the criminal being apprehended in Fargo is overall irrelevant in the context of the story. It’s not about how law enforcement is successful in arresting a criminal, but about how the events lead the characters to get a first-hand experience of the chaos and violence that’s out there, and how their personal spaces, where they resort to at the end of the movie, are still a sanctuary against the barbaric acts that we just witnessed.

Oh I agree, I just think that what makes the arrest impactful is the speech Marge has in the car about how all this happened just for "a little bit of money". It comments on the events of the film, how they might have all been better off if they, like Norm and Marge, be satisfied with their lives.

And in terms of Jerry and Moss, one is a stupid car salesman and the other is a competent and experienced ‘Nam vet. I thought you said these things don’t matter?

And Mills does play the same function, if we’re being so broad, as the dude in over his head, who thinks he can take the bad guys on to get what he wants but ultimately is undone.

As for that strawman about me attacking the Coens, you’re again missing the point. The Coens aren’t lazy; they’re just making crime films and the roles you identified in your post are incredibly broad and apply to *tons* of crime films. I’ve been saying this consistently.

>And in terms of Jerry and Moss, one is a stupid car salesman and the other is a competent and experienced ‘Nam vet. I thought you said these things don’t matter?

In the overall context of the story, they don’t. They’re both amateur criminals hoping they can get away. Jerry and Moss are dumb shits. They’re an example of a guy - usually not an evil guy - who does stupid crimes because he makes foolish choices for their own personal gain. They are contrasted to the pure evil impersonations that their movies present. Brad Pitt is not to a contrast to Kevin Spacey, but to Morgan Freeman. There are two different version of righteousness, instead of two versions of evilness.

To be clear, I’m not saying that any of these characters are identical.

I’m talking about the function they play in the story, if we’re abstracting to the level of the OP.
I think the function is inherently different, but you're well within your rights to disagree. I personally enjoy the discussion!
Not unless we abstract to an unhelpful level, which is my point.

>Not unless we abstract to an unhelpful level, which is my point.

I brought forward a discussion about two films. The same way I could make a case about Sofia Coppola's Virgin Suicide and Marie Antoinette being thematically similar examples of teenage boredom. And you could go on with: but isn't this movie of this other director an example of this? And we could keep debating to the end of our goddamn lives.
I’m not debating. I’m pointing out that the pieces you identified as supposedly linking these two films in a remarkable way are just basic building blocks found in *tons* of crime flicks.
Yet you brought forward Seven as an example that didn't hold up.
Except that it does.
You can have the last word, I won't make me my point again.

It is actually uncanny how closely the script in No Country for Old Men adheres to the book. You know the age old question - what's better, the movie or the book? In this case I read the book after seeing the movie and essentially got nothing more out of the book than I'd already seen in the movie.

Llewelyn initiates the game though. Sure, he loses and yes I agree, he isn’t an idiot. Still, he is “the fool” for entering a game that plays by no rules while refusing to veer from his own set of rules.

To call Moss a fool is a misreading the character. He goes back to the crime scene because he feels guilty for abandoning that man to die. Jerry is a desperate man, frustrated by life, who gets way above his head when he decides to do something. Neither of them think of themselves as clever. Both eventually find themselves in situations out of their control, but that is hardly unique to these two films or the Coens. It’s a well worn trope that has been around since storytelling started. I think you are finding parallels because you know both were made by the Coens. But the two films are not really about the same thing.
Sure, and as I was saying to OP, they’ve really just identified three basic building blocks of a crime flick: the cop, the villain, and the guy in the jackpot.

This is an interesting POV, but it doesn't really hang together for me, beyond agreeing that the Coen brothers were attracted with both stories to a similar kind of morality tale.

First and foremost for me against your take, however, is that while Macy's character in FARGO is a fool, Llewellyn in NCFOM is NOT a fool, but a very smart, capable man whose pride or arrogance simply allows him to underestimate his opponent.

I also have a different read on both endings -- I would rather describe it not so much as Marge being "toughened up" by the events, but that she has emerged unscathed, with her essential goodness intact.

Whereas, to me, Sheriff Ed Tom is damaged by what he has witnessed. He has lost belief. It is only in the telling of his dreams to his wife that we (and his wife) see that there is still hope within him, even if he cannot see it yet.

I have a lot more I could say about NCFOM because in its own way there is something really beautiful and solemn in its grandeur about that film to me. Llewelyn's death is sad and tawdry -- he isn't even killed by his rival. His own hubris defeats him. Whereas Carla Jean is killed by Chigurh but not defeated by him. She knows he is a hollow man and she reveals that to him. Then immediately after, like a stroke from God, he is hit by a car like the hammer of God, as if in retribution. There is again something like the touch of the divine when Ed Tom, thinking himself in despair, is sent dreams in which it does seem to me that God (or the spirit of his father) is directly attempting to give him comfort. That the world still holds hope, and warmth, and a fire ahead.

I just think it's more complicated than distilling everyone down to an archetype.
Doesn't Llewelyn take the money when he first sees it though? I agree with your take on the character but the tracker in the suitcase was his downfall from the beginning right?

Before Llewelyn finds the money he comes across a dying man who is begging for water which he is unable to give him as he seems not to have any (a bit strange since he is out in the Texas sun).

If I remember correctly after he has taken the money - is it from a corpse under a tree - back to where he lives he later returns to the crime scene with water but the dying man has indeed died.

The tracker does lead “sugar” to him.

In defense of OP's reaching comparison of the two great films - I do believe Llewelyn is not the brightest bulb. Both the book and the film indicate as much. Further, he was outmatched from the intro scenes.

Moss, (his name is important) wings the animal he's hunting - so he's not a great hunter or marksman. He is an urban cowboy who wears the wrong boots for the terrain. All these things are important and intentional. 

Moss is also inferred to be impotent. Threatening to take his girl Carla Jean into the bedroom and screw her, she replies "big talk."

In the Mexican hospital, Carson Wells asks Moss about his skills, including welding and immediately talks down to him, asking "Mig, tig, braise, pot-metal?" Wells doesn't respect Moss for anything but his surviving as long as he has. Wells again saying, "your not cut out for this. You're just some guy..."

Moss *literally* does foolish things, first by taking the money, and second by returning to the massacre *in his truck* to give water to a gutshot and dying man from the day before. If you steal millions in cartel money you do not return to the scene of the bloody crime. What Moss does is stupid and he even admits his actions are stupid.

Admitting his failures and stupidity doesn't save him or Carla Jean. His initial foolish actions doom them both from the start. 

Moss thought he was a smart guy who made a few mistakes but could still get away with his theft. He was dead wrong.

To quote an old poker game adage, *If you look around the card table and can't find the donkey, then the donkey is you.*

Not to take anything away from their masterful cannon - but they will never make a better film than Blood Simple. The brothers came out fully formed masterful storytellers. 

Leaves me with serious Altman-esque MASH vibes.
Yeah it's stunning they made it without any task training, just their genius and talent.

The biker represents racism in the US by wearing the Peckerwood tattoo that Hi also carries -

https://www.adl.org/resources/hate-symbol/peckerwood

He does take it when he first sees it, but then he returns to the scene later on. There he has to abandon his truck because the Mexicans with the pitbull attack him.

It is only because he leaves his truck that Chigurh gets the registration from the truck, which leads him to Moss' trailer, where he picks up Moss' phone bill, and eventually tracks down where he is likely to be staying from the phone records.

It is only when he gets within a few hundred metres of Moss' hotel room does the tracker start working.

He may have gotten away with it, or at the very least had a much bigger head start, if he didn't go back to the drug deal and have to abandon his truck.
"Sugar"? What are you talking about?
When Llewelyn speaks to Carson Wells he pronounces Anton Chigurh as “sugar”.
